title: The Cervicovaginal Microbiome
abstract: The cervicovaginal microbiome (CVM) is a dynamic ecological system that plays a central role in women’s reproductive and sexual health. The current accepted perspective characterizes the optimal CVM as being dominated by lactic acid‐producing Lactobacillus species, which maintain an acidic vaginal environment and suppress colonization by pathogens. Dysbiosis, most commonly manifested as bacterial vaginosis (BV), is characterized by the depletion of Lactobacillus and the overgrowth of anaerobic bacteria such as Gardnerella vaginalis and Candidatus Lachnocurva vaginae (formerly known as BVAB1). BV affects roughly one‐third of reproductive‐aged women (and more in high-risk populations), and it has been repeatedly observed to associate with infertility, adverse pregnancy outcomes, an increased risk of sexually transmitted infections (STIs), and postmenopausal status. Advances in high‐throughput sequencing have revealed that CVM communities segregate into discrete categorical community state types (CSTs), and that molecular tools such as molecular BV ( molBV ) can reproduce Nugent scoring to generate a molecular diagnosis of BV (mBV) while uncovering clinically relevant subtypes. Emerging evidence links specific CSTs and mBV subtypes to persistent high‐risk human papillomavirus (hrHPV) infection, cervical pre‐cancer, and Chlamydia trachomatis acquisition (Ravel, J., Gajer, P., Abdo, Z., Schneider, G. Vaginal microbiome of reproductive-age women. Proc Natl Acad Sci U S A, 108(Suppl 1), 4680–4687. doi:10.1073/pnas.1002611107; Usyk, M., Carlson, L., Schlecht, N. C., Grassi, E., Wiek, F., ... Cervicovaginal microbiome and natural history of C. trachomatis in adolescents and young women. Cell; Usyk, M., Schlecht, N. F., Pickering, S., Williams, L., Sollecito, C. C., Gradissimo, A., ... molBV reveals immune landscape of bacterial vaginosis and predicts human papillomavirus infection natural history. Nature C ommunications, 13(1), 1–12). This chapter reviews the ecology of the CVM, key bacterial constituents, epidemiology across populations, and recent methodological advances, while highlighting the public‐health importance of microbiome–host interactions.

title: Knowledge, attitude, and practice regarding HPV vaccination and cervical cancer prevention among healthcare providers at a tertiary care hospital: A cross-sectional study
abstract: Background: Human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccination is a key component of cervical cancer prevention, and healthcare providers play an important role in communicating vaccine-related information and encouraging preventive practices. Knowledge gaps among healthcare personnel may influence their ability to counsel patients and advocate vaccination. Objectives: The objective of this study is to assess the knowledge, attitudes, and practices regarding HPV vaccination and cervical cancer prevention among healthcare providers at a tertiary care hospital. Methods: A descriptive cross-sectional Knowledge, Attitude, and Practice (KAP) study was conducted at DVVPF’s Medical College and Hospital, Ahilyanagar, over a 6-month period, on 200 participants to assess awareness, perceptions, and behaviours related to HPV vaccination and cancer prevention. The study was carried out among healthcare workers (including students) using a structured, pre-tested questionnaire consisting of three sections: knowledge about HPV infection and vaccination, attitudes toward HPV vaccination, and practices related to vaccination and cancer screening. Results: Among the 200 healthcare providers surveyed, the majority were females (68%), belonged to the HPV vaccine-eligible age group of 18-26 years (60%), and were predominantly doctors (49.5%), followed by paramedical staff (27%) and nurses (23.5%). Overall awareness of HPV and its mode of transmission was high across genders and age groups. Females showed slightly better knowledge regarding HPV vaccination, its availability in India, and related aspects compared to males. Participants older than 26 years demonstrated higher knowledge levels than younger respondents regarding vaccine availability, recommended age group, vaccine types, and HPV strains associated with cervical cancer. Doctors exhibited the highest awareness across almost all domains of HPV infection and vaccination, followed by paramedical staff, while nurses showed comparatively less awareness. Conclusion: HPV vaccination remains one of the most impactful strategies in preventing cervical cancer. Low knowledge levels can be attributed to very low vaccine coverage, despite its availability in open markets. Strategies such as health education through mass media concerning HPV vaccination and cervical cancer may be implemented.
journal: International Journal of Clinical Obstetrics and Gynaecology

title: Adjuvant Nonavalent HPV Vaccination is Associated with Improved One-Year HPV Clearance and Cervical Cytological Outcomes in Women with Histopathologically Confirmed LSIL/CIN1: A Retrospective Comparative Cohort Study
abstract: Purpose: To compare one-year human papilloma virus (HPV) deoxyribonucleic acid and cervical cytology outcomes between women with histopathologically confirmed low-grade squamous intraepithelial lesions/cervical intraepithelial neoplasia grade 1 (LSIL/CIN1) who received adjuvant nonavalent HPV vaccination and a contemporaneous unvaccinated control cohort, and to identify baseline predictors of persistent disease.Methods: This single-center retrospective comparative cohort study included women with histopathologically confirmed LSIL/ CIN1, divided into vaccinated and unvaccinated (control) subgroups, who were treated between 2020 and 2025.The primary outcomes were one-year HPV clearance and cytological normalization.Complete regression was defined as concurrent HPV negativity and normal cervical cytology, whereas persistent disease was defined as persistent HPV positivity together with abnormal cervical cytology.Univariable logistic regression analysis was performed to identify predictors of persistent disease in the vaccinated cohort.Results: Of the study cohort of 233 women, 153 (65.7%) women completed the three-dose nonavalent HPV vaccination schedule, while 80 (34.3%) women served as controls.Baseline demographic and clinical characteristics were comparable between the groups.At 12 months, HPV clearance was significantly more prevalent in the vaccinated group than in the control group (70.6% vs. 52.5%,p=0.009).Cytological normalization was also more frequent in vaccinated women (72.5% vs. 26.2%,p<0.001).Complete regression occurred in 53.6% of vaccinated women compared with 16.2% of controls (p<0.001),and consequently persistent disease was significantly less common in the vaccinated group (10.5% vs. 37.5%, p<0.001).Although HPV16, HPV18, other high-risk HPV types, and multiple HPV infections decreased in both groups, genotype-specific differences were not statistically significant.Baseline HPV18 positivity was the only significant predictor of persistent disease (odds ratio: 3.97, 95% confidence interval: 1.29-12.24;p=0.017).Conclusion: Adjuvant nonavalent HPV vaccination was associated with higher HPV clearance, improved cervical cytological outcomes, higher complete regression, and lower persistent disease rates in women with histopathologically confirmed LSIL/ CIN1.Prospective multicenter studies are warranted to confirm these findings and further define the role of adjuvant HPV vaccination in the conservative management of LSIL/CIN1.

title: Corrigendum to “Degenerate cysteine patterns mediate two redox sensing mechanisms in the papillomavirus E7 oncoprotein” [Redox Biol. 11 (2017) 38-50]
abstract: This Corrigendum relates to the above article.Post-publication, an investigation identified a concern around the authenticity of the following image panel:• Fig. 5 Panel C (Oxidation of HPV16 E7Δ1-26 (C68A) resolved by RP-HPLC -pH 9.0) and Fig. 5 Panel C (Oxidation of HPV16 E7Δ1-26 (C68A) resolved by RP-HPLC -pH 8.0) depict the same source image, but are described as representing different experimental samples.The authors were requested to provide comment on these concerns, as well as the original unprocessed image files to aid investigation, and have clarified that the chromatogram shown in Fig. 5C for pH 8.0 is identical to the chromatogram shown for pH 9.0.The authors identified an error in the preparation of the waterfall plot.During figure assembly, the chromatogram corresponding to pH 9.0 was inserted twice, resulting in duplication of the pH 9.0 trace and omission of the pH 8.0 trace.The chromatogram shown for pH 9.0 is the correct chromatogram for that condition.The chromatogram for pH 8.0 was therefore incorrectly represented in the published figure.The figure has been corrected by replacing the duplicated pH 9.0 trace with the chromatogram corresponding to pH 8.0.The authors have provided the correct Fig. 5 as below.The authors apologise for this oversight.
